patient.name: Walter Simmons
patient.chiefComplaint: Weakness and dizziness; family found him slow to respond with a slow pulse

history.hpi: 70-year-old male found by his daughter slumped in his recliner, unusually drowsy and slow to respond. She states he has seemed "off" and weak since this afternoon. An empty bottle of metoprolol tartrate 100 mg, refilled 3 days ago, was found on the side table with far fewer pills remaining than expected. Patient is arousable to voice, denies chest pain, admits to feeling "foggy" and lightheaded. No witnessed seizure, no vomiting.
history.lastOralIntake: Light dinner approximately 5 hours prior to onset
history.events: Daughter last spoke with patient by phone around 1730 hrs and he sounded normal. She arrived at 1930 hrs to find him slumped in his recliner, difficult to arouse, with an empty metoprolol bottle on the side table. She called 911 immediately. Unclear if ingestion was accidental double-dosing or intentional; daughter reports he has seemed depressed lately.

scene.dispatch: Difficulty breathing / weak person, 70-year-old male, unable to be roused easily, private residence
scene.location: Single-family home, living room recliner, first floor
scene.safety: Scene safe, no hazards identified; daughter present and cooperative
scene.bystanders: Daughter present on scene; called 911 after finding patient unusually drowsy and slow to respond. Reports empty metoprolol bottle on the side table and possible worsening depression.
visualCues: Empty metoprolol tartrate 100 mg prescription bottle on end table, refill dated 3 days prior
Patient pale, diaphoretic, sitting slumped in recliner
Half-empty water glass on side table
Patient slow to track conversation, speech mildly slurred

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 70-year-old male slumped in his recliner, pale and diaphoretic, slow to arouse. Radial pulses are slow and weak. Family reports an empty metoprolol bottle and possible overdose.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present but slow, thready, and weak; skin pale, cool, diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities on command, slow to respond
otherFindings: Bradycardic pulse noted on initial palpation
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I just feel... really foggy... and dizzy."

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize symptomatic bradycardia (HR 38 with hypotension and AMS)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Heart rate less than 60 beats per minute (BPM) with either symptoms (altered mental status (AMS), chest pain (CP), congestive heart failure (CHF), seizure, syncope, shock, pallor, diaphoresis) or evidence of hemodynamic instability
expectedActions.rationale: Establishes inclusion criteria for the Bradycardia guideline and drives urgency of treatment.

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain ingestion history (drug, time, quantity) and collect the pill bottle to bring to the ED
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Obtain an accurate ingestion history (as patient may become unconscious before arrival at the emergency department (ED)): Time of ingestion or exposure Route of exposure Quantity of medication or toxin taken (safely collect all possible medications or agents) Alcohol or other intoxicant taken
expectedActions.rationale: Identifies beta-blocker overdose as the likely etiology and informs time-sensitive treatment decisions (e.g., charcoal eligibility).

expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer oxygen as appropriate with a target of achieving 94–98% saturation
expectedActions.rationale: Corrects hypoxia as a contributing cause of bradycardia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate cardiac monitor and obtain 12-lead EKG
expectedActions.rationale: Confirms rhythm and rules out ischemic cause of bradycardia.
Required for medication and fluid administration.

expectedActions.shortAction: Check blood glucose (beta-blockers can cause hypoglycemia)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Check blood glucose level on all patients but especially on pediatric patients as beta-blockers can cause hypoglycemia in pediatric population
expectedActions.rationale: Rules out hypoglycemia as contributing/confounding cause of AMS and bradycardia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Atropine 1 mg IV push (fixed adult dose; may repeat q5min to max 3 mg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider atropine sulfate for symptomatic bradycardia Adult: Atropine 1 mg IV q 5 minutes to maximum of 3 mg
expectedActions.rationale: First-line pharmacologic therapy for symptomatic bradycardia; expected to have limited effect in beta-blocker overdose.

transitions.condition: Crew completes the primary assessment, confirms symptomatic bradycardia, and gives atropine 1 mg IV per the Bradycardia guideline.

phases.name: Atropine Given
phases.description: Crew manages airway, applies oxygen and the cardiac monitor, obtains a 12-lead EKG, establishes IV access, checks blood glucose, and administers atropine per the Bradycardia and Beta Blocker Overdose guidelines. HR and BP show minimal improvement.
phases.triggerCondition: Primary survey confirms symptomatic bradycardia (HR 38, BP 78/50, AMS). Crew initiates standard bradycardia management and gives a first dose of atropine.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, oxygen applied via nasal cannula
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses slow and weak; IV established in left AC
otherFindings: 12-lead EKG confirms sinus bradycardia, no ST elevation
No response in mentation to atropine

expectedActions.shortAction: Glucagon 5 mg IVP (fixed adult dose; may repeat in 5-10 min, max 10 mg total)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For symptomatic patients with cardiac effects (e.g., hypotension, bradycardia) consider: Adult: Glucagon initial dose 5 mg IVP — this can be repeated in 5–10 minutes for a total of 10 mg
expectedActions.rationale: Glucagon bypasses beta-receptor blockade to increase heart rate and contractility, making it a targeted antidote for beta-blocker toxicity.

expectedActions.shortAction: Normal saline bolus 1,680 mL IV (84 kg x 20 mL/kg) for hypotension
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider fluid challenge (20 mL/kg) for hypotension with associated bradycardia
expectedActions.rationale: Supports blood pressure while awaiting response to glucagon and prepares for potential vasopressor need.

expectedActions.shortAction: Defer activated charcoal - ingestion occurred approximately 2 hours prior, outside 1-hour window
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider activated charcoal without sorbitol (1 g/kg) PO only if within the first hour of ingestion, if indicated per the time of ingestion. If risk of rapid decreasing mental status, do not administer oral agent without adequately protecting the airway
expectedActions.rationale: Reinforces that charcoal is time-limited and airway-status dependent; correctly withholding it here demonstrates protocol understanding.

transitions.condition: HR remains under 50 and BP remains under 90 systolic despite atropine 1 mg IV; crew recognizes atropine is unlikely to be effective in beta-blocker toxicity and escalates to glucagon per the Beta Blocker Poisoning/Overdose guideline.
Crew re-doses atropine repeatedly without moving to glucagon or transcutaneous pacing despite persistent hemodynamic instability; treatment escalation is delayed more than 5 minutes.

phases.name: Glucagon Given
phases.description: Atropine has little effect, consistent with beta-blocker toxicity. Crew administers glucagon and a fluid bolus for hypotension. HR and BP improve modestly but the patient remains symptomatic.
phases.triggerCondition: After atropine 1 mg IV, HR remains in the high 30s-low 40s and BP remains under 90 systolic. Crew recognizes atropine may have little or no effect in beta-blocker overdose and escalates per the Beta Blocker Poisoning/Overdose guideline.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses slightly stronger, still slow; fluid bolus running
otherFindings: No significant change in QRS width on repeat EKG
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel a little sick to my stomach now."

expectedActions.shortAction: Administer sedation/analgesia prior to transcutaneous pacing
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transcutaneous Pacing – If pacing is performed, consider sedation or pain control
expectedActions.rationale: Pacing is painful; sedation improves patient tolerance and cooperation.

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate transcutaneous pacing at 70 bpm; titrate mA until electrical and mechanical capture confirmed
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider transcutaneous pacing if refractory to initial pharmacologic interventions
expectedActions.rationale: Provides mechanical chronotropic support when pharmacologic therapy fails to correct hemodynamically significant bradycardia.

transitions.condition: Despite glucagon 5 mg IVP and a 1,680 mL crystalloid bolus, HR remains under 50 and BP remains under 90 systolic. Crew proceeds to transcutaneous pacing per the Beta Blocker Poisoning/Overdose and Bradycardia guidelines.

phases.name: TCP Initiated
phases.description: Bradycardia and hypotension are refractory to atropine, glucagon, and fluids. Crew provides sedation and initiates transcutaneous pacing, achieving electrical and mechanical capture, with improvement in heart rate and blood pressure.
phases.triggerCondition: HR and BP remain critically low despite atropine, glucagon, and a fluid bolus. Per the Beta Blocker Poisoning/Overdose guideline, transcutaneous pacing is initiated as refractory to initial pharmacologic interventions.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses stronger and regular at paced rate
otherFindings: Electrical and mechanical capture confirmed with pacer at 70 bpm, 80 mA
Sedation given prior to pacing; patient tolerating pacing well
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "That thumping feeling is odd, but I feel a bit clearer now."

expectedActions.shortAction: Consider norepinephrine infusion 1.7-33.6 mcg/min IV (84 kg x 0.02-0.4 mcg/kg/min) titrated to MAP >65 mmHg if hypotension persists after pacing
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider vasopressors after adequate fluid resuscitation (1–2 liters of crystalloid) for the hypotensive patient
expectedActions.rationale: Addresses persistent hypotension that pacing alone may not correct, since pacing may not always correct blood pressure even with successful capture.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess capture, pulse quality, and blood pressure response to pacing
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transcutaneous pacing may not always capture nor correct hypotension when capture is successful
expectedActions.rationale: Confirms pacing is mechanically effective and identifies need for additional vasopressor support.

phases.name: TCP Delayed
phases.description: Crew continues to re-dose atropine rather than escalating to glucagon and transcutaneous pacing. The patient's heart rate and blood pressure continue to fall and mental status deteriorates toward unresponsiveness.
phases.triggerCondition: Atropine is repeated without escalation to glucagon or transcutaneous pacing for more than 5 minutes despite ongoing hemodynamic instability. HR and BP continue to fall and the patient's mental status deteriorates.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but at risk; increasing secretions
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses weak and thready, barely palpable; central pulses only
otherFindings: No improvement despite repeated atropine dosing
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Moans to painful stimuli, no longer forming words

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize refractory bradycardia; escalate immediately to glucagon and transcutaneous pacing
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Bradycardia should be managed via the least invasive manner possible, escalating care as needed In cases of impending hemodynamic collapse, proceed directly to transcutaneous pacing
expectedActions.rationale: Repeated atropine without escalation delays definitive therapy and allows continued hemodynamic deterioration in beta-blocker toxicity, where atropine is frequently ineffective.
